children: Goldman Sachs says the U.S. stock market has an unusual combination of strong headline performance and weak investor conviction, creating the potential for further gains and a catch-up rally among stocks left behind by the market’s AI leaders.
The S&P 500 (

) has gained 14% this year, yet Goldman’s U.S. Equity Sentiment Indicator has fallen to -0.9, matching its March low. The indicator combines nine measures of positioning among institutional, retail and foreign investors. Goldman strategist Ben Snider and his team said in a Sept. 25 report that the reading leaves investors with room to increase equity exposure if the economic backdrop improves.
The weakness beneath the index is even more striking. The S&P 500 (

) recently traded just 1% below its August record, while the median constituent was 16% below its own 52-week high. Goldman’s preferred measure of market breadth has fallen to its lowest level since the Dot-Com Bubble.

For investors, that divergence could matter if uncertainty around interest rates and economic growth recedes. Goldman sees scope for both broad market upside and a rebound among lagging stocks, although unusually narrow breadth could also produce continued volatility in momentum trades.
S&P 500 valuation has fallen despite the rally
The market has become less expensive even as stock prices have risen. The S&P 500's (

) forward price-to-earnings ratio has contracted to about 19 times earnings, roughly in line with its 10-year average. Consensus forward earnings estimates have risen much faster than the index itself, pushing the multiple down sharply from a year ago.
Higher interest rates are one reason. The real 10-year Treasury yield
climbed 53 basis points over the month covered by the report. Goldman said the speed of that increase crossed a threshold that historically has been associated with weaker equity returns.

Goldman estimates the S&P 500's (SP500) current 19 times multiple is about 10% below the level suggested by its model of interest rates, inflation and corporate profitability. The strategists do not interpret that discount as evidence of an excessively gloomy earnings outlook. Instead, they believe investors are questioning whether today's exceptionally high profit levels can persist.
AI spending is boosting profits, but the lift may fade
That skepticism is particularly important because of the AI investment boom.

Goldman estimates hyperscalers are on pace to spend $800 billion on capital expenditures this year. That spending is flowing into revenue and profits for semiconductor companies and other AI infrastructure suppliers. The firm estimates hyperscaler capex is responsible for roughly half of S&P 500 (SP500) earnings growth this year.

But the benefit may not last at its current magnitude. As growth in AI capital spending slows and depreciation costs rise, Goldman expects the contribution to S&P 500 (SP500) earnings growth to fade and eventually become a drag. Supply shortages that have supported semiconductor margins could also become less helpful.

That helps explain a seeming contradiction in today's market. Stocks look reasonably valued based on near-term earnings, but expensive when profits are viewed over a longer horizon. The cyclically adjusted P/E based on 10 years of earnings is near historical extremes, below the 1999-2000 peak but above its 2021 level.

Free cash flow paints a less extreme picture. Goldman calculates a U.S. equity market free cash flow yield of 3.3%, below its historical median of 4.4% but comparable with levels seen during several other periods in recent decades.
Profitability is driving valuations
Corporate profitability has become unusually important in determining which parts of the market command premium valuations.

Goldman found that nearly all the current variation in sector price-to-book multiples can be explained by differences in return on equity. The relationship between sector profitability and valuations is now among the strongest seen in decades.

The S&P 500's (SP500) return on equity is currently around 24%. Goldman calculates that today's 19 times forward P/E would be consistent with an ROE closer to 22%, suggesting the market is already pricing in some retreat from unusually high profitability.

The firm's analysis also suggests that the recent run in value stocks may become harder to sustain. Goldman's sector-neutral long-short Value factor has gained more than 25% since mid-2025. But valuation differences across stocks have narrowed, while Goldman economists expect stable, near-trend economic growth. Both conditions have historically been less favorable for the Value factor.
Investors are looking further into the future
At the individual-stock level, Goldman found a notable change in what investors are willing to pay for.

Long-term revenue growth has become especially important. Investors are assigning an above-average valuation premium to expected sales growth three years into the future while putting less weight than usual on one-year sales growth.

That shift may reflect doubts about the reliability of near-term earnings as a guide to long-term value. The AI investment cycle has temporarily lifted profits for some companies while AI itself could threaten the future earnings of others.
The result is a market increasingly focused on a basic question: which companies can keep growing after today's unusual conditions normalize?
Goldman still sees S&P 500 upside
Despite the risks, Goldman's broader market forecasts remain constructive.

The firm forecasts S&P 500 (SP500) earnings of $375 a share in 2026 and $415 in 2027. Its year-end 2026 S&P 500 target is 8,000, about 4% above the level used in the report. Its 12-month target of 8,700 implies a roughly 13% gain.

The investment backdrop is therefore more nuanced than the index's performance alone suggests. The S&P 500 (SP500) has risen sharply, but its valuation multiple has fallen. Investor positioning is light, market breadth is historically narrow and profitability remains exceptionally high.

For investors, Goldman's analysis suggests the next leg of the market may depend less on another expansion in valuations and more on whether earnings can justify them. If macro uncertainty declines, sidelined capital and depressed positioning could provide fuel for gains beyond the stocks that have dominated the AI rally. But persistent high rates or a sharper normalization in AI-driven profits could test whether today's 19 times earnings multiple is as moderate as it first appears.

title: Goldman Sachs sees room for S&P 500 gains as investor positioning sinks
